outcomes: Explain UTF-8 byte sequences without conflating bytes, token IDs, or Unicode scalar values
Fit deterministic non-overlapping BPE merge rules from adjacent counts
Encode bytes to token IDs and decode token IDs to the exact original bytes
Relate maximum merge count, learned rule count, and vocabulary size
Serialize merge order and reject malformed tokenizer files

utf-8.name: UTF-8
utf-8.definition: A variable-length Unicode encoding using one to four bytes per scalar value.
utf-8.explanation: UTF-8 preserves ASCII byte values and represents other Unicode scalar values with multi-byte sequences. Rust strings guarantee valid UTF-8, but a byte vector may contain incomplete or invalid sequences. Token boundaries in byte BPE can split a multi-byte character, so decoding each token independently as text is unsafe. Concatenate token bytes first and validate the complete result when a text boundary requires it. Byte counts, token counts, and Unicode scalar-value counts therefore answer different questions and should always be labeled.

byte-pair-encoding.name: byte-pair encoding
byte-pair-encoding.definition: A tokenizer fitted by repeatedly replacing frequent adjacent symbol pairs with new symbols.
byte-pair-encoding.explanation: Byte BPE starts with 256 symbols, one for every byte, and estimates an ordered list of merge rules from adjacent counts. Each new token represents the concatenation of two earlier tokens. Encoding begins from bytes and applies rules by learned rank; decoding concatenates stored byte strings. The byte base guarantees coverage and exact round trips. The maximum merge count, actual rule count, merge order, boundary policy, tie-breaking, pre-tokenization, and normalization are part of tokenizer identity because changing them can change token IDs consumed by a model.

round-trip.name: round trip
round-trip.definition: The invariant that decoding an encoded byte sequence reproduces the original bytes exactly.
round-trip.explanation: A round-trip test compares bytes rather than displayed strings: decode(encode(bytes)) must equal bytes. It catches overlapping replacements, incorrect learned-token bytes, invalid IDs, and serialization-order mistakes. Multilingual examples are valuable because UTF-8 characters span different byte lengths and token boundaries may split them. Exact round trip establishes reversibility, not compression quality or model accuracy. A reloaded tokenizer should satisfy the same invariant and produce identical token IDs when deterministic compatibility matters.

sources.title: Neural Machine Translation of Rare Words with Subword Units
Language Models are Unsupervised Multitask Learners

checks: The default fixture requests at most 24 merge rules, learns 12, and produces a 268-entry vocabulary
Multilingual byte round trips pass for ASCII, accented text, CJK, and emoji
Saved and reloaded merge tables are equal
Malformed headers, forward references, oversized expansion, and unknown token IDs return errors
Starter prints Unicode scalar-value and UTF-8 byte counts before its guided test
limitations: Repeated scans are O(merge rules × current tokens)
The fitting API treats one supplied byte slice as one document and omits production pre-tokenization
The text serialization has no checksum
